groups.title: Passage 1 · A library of things · Questions 1–15
groups.text:
A. Before the city of Bellhaven opened its first library of things, residents could borrow books but not the equipment needed to maintain their homes. Buying a drill for a single afternoon seemed wasteful, yet commercial hire shops mainly served professional builders and required expensive deposits. A neighbourhood survey found that householders were more interested in borrowing practical equipment than in attending additional workshops. The council therefore converted a vacant room beside the public library into a lending service. It opened in March 2017 with ninety donated objects, ranging from carpet cleaners to sewing machines. Its purpose was to reduce unnecessary purchases rather than to generate a profit. A small membership fee was introduced to pay for maintenance, but residents receiving certain benefits could join free.

B. The organisers initially predicted that gardening equipment would be most popular. In practice, carpet cleaners were requested more often than any other category. The result reflected the large number of rented flats in the area: tenants wanted to clean before moving out, while many had no garden. Some objects attracted surprisingly little interest. A pasta machine was borrowed twice in its first year, despite attracting many enthusiastic comments at the launch. Staff learned that what people admire publicly and what they actually need are not always the same. They began asking members about upcoming tasks rather than showing them attractive products and requesting opinions. This changed both purchasing decisions and the wording of publicity materials.

C. Borrowing rules also evolved. During the first six months, everything could be kept for seven days. Members complained that weekend-only projects did not require a whole week, whereas sewing projects sometimes took longer. The service eventually introduced different loan periods for different categories. A deposit remained compulsory for especially valuable items, but ordinary members did not need a deposit for basic tools. Late returns caused more difficulties than broken items: an object that appeared available online could still be in somebody's kitchen when the next borrower arrived. Automated reminders helped, but staff also reserved a day between consecutive bookings for inspections. Consequently, an item was not always bookable immediately after its scheduled return.

D. Maintaining the collection required expertise that the original volunteers did not all possess. Two retired engineers began a weekly repair session, and a local college supplied supervised students. The partnership gave students experience with genuine faults rather than carefully prepared classroom demonstrations. Every electrical item was inspected after each loan, even when the borrower reported no problem. Items that failed inspection were removed from the catalogue until repaired. The service did not invite members to mend electrical faults themselves. However, it offered a short introductory session on safe operation before lending unfamiliar equipment. Attendance was compulsory for some machines but optional for ordinary hand tools. Records of repairs gradually revealed which brands were economical over their entire working life, not merely cheap to acquire.

E. The environmental benefits were harder to establish than the borrowing statistics. A lending transaction does not automatically replace a purchase: without the service, some members might simply have postponed their project or borrowed from a relative. Researcher Maya Chen interviewed 120 members and asked what they would otherwise have done. She estimated that approximately half of the loans replaced purchases, while warning that the sample was voluntary and might overrepresent environmentally motivated residents. Her study did not compare Bellhaven with another city. Nor did it measure the energy used in manufacturing every object. Chen recommended reporting several indicators, including utilisation, repairs and avoided purchases, rather than presenting one impressive but uncertain carbon-saving figure.

F. In 2022, a grant allowed the service to extend its opening hours to two evenings a week. Members working during ordinary library hours then used it more often. The grant did not fund a larger collection; staff argued that access mattered more than adding objects which would sit unused. Membership rose, but the council declined an offer from a retailer to install advertisements in the borrowing room. Managers wanted advice to remain independent of sales. They still bought replacement items from several suppliers and published their selection principles. The next planned improvement was a shared reservation system with two nearby neighbourhoods. It would increase access to specialist equipment without requiring each branch to own an identical collection.

groups.title: Passage 2 · Light with a purpose · Questions 16–28
groups.text:
A. For decades, city administrations have treated street lighting as a straightforward question of visibility: brighter streets were assumed to be better streets. Yet the introduction of efficient LED lamps has reopened a more complicated debate. A lamp that consumes fewer watts can still produce a great deal of unwanted light. If its lower running cost encourages a city to install more lamps or operate them for longer, total energy savings may be smaller than predicted. Researchers call this a rebound effect. It does not mean that efficient technology is useless. It means that the benefits of efficiency depend partly on decisions made after installation, including how much illumination users consider necessary.

B. Light can be directed more precisely than older systems allowed. A well-designed fitting illuminates a pavement without sending much light into bedroom windows or directly into the sky. This distinction matters because total brightness is a poor description of lighting quality. A powerful lamp shining into a pedestrian's eyes can reduce the ability to see an uneven surface beyond it. Engineers describe such discomfort as glare. Shielding the source and controlling its angle may improve visibility even when measured output is lower. Some city councils now assess whether a light serves a specific task instead of applying the same standard to every street, park and car park.

C. Ecological concerns have also changed the discussion. Artificial light at night can alter the behaviour of insects, birds and other animals. In a fictional field trial near Lanton, researchers compared riverbank sites under three types of lamp. Blue-rich white lamps attracted more flying insects than warmer lamps, although the difference varied with weather. Removing lights altogether had a larger effect than changing their colour. The team emphasised that the experiment examined attraction to lamps, not long-term changes in insect populations. A lower count at a particular lamp therefore did not prove that more insects survived across the whole landscape. Similar care is needed when drawing conclusions about birds from observations on a single illuminated building.

D. Public safety is often invoked as a reason to resist dimming. However, correlations between lighting and recorded crime can be difficult to interpret. Wealthier districts may have both newer lights and other investments such as better transport or staffed public spaces. When a council changes lighting, it may also increase police patrols. A subsequent decline in crime cannot automatically be attributed to the lamps. This uncertainty does not justify ignoring residents' concerns. Rather, it suggests that evaluations should include comparable areas and record other changes during the study. Perceived safety also matters because fear can stop people using a route even when recorded incidents are rare. A technically efficient scheme that nobody trusts may fail in practice.

E. In the fictional town of Norbridge, a pilot project dimmed selected residential streetlights after midnight rather than switching them off. The council excluded road junctions and pedestrian crossings. Before the trial, residents walked the routes with engineers and identified places where trees blocked the light. Pruning branches solved several problems without adding brighter lamps. The council then collected feedback through both an online questionnaire and paper forms at the library, since an online-only survey would have excluded some residents. Most respondents accepted the dimming, but people working night shifts asked for a well-lit connection between the bus stop and the main road. That section was subsequently removed from the pilot.

F. Smart controls provide another possibility. Sensors can increase output when a pedestrian approaches and reduce it afterwards. Nevertheless, buying sensors introduces costs of its own: equipment must be maintained, software supported and faults investigated. A control system that works well in a demonstration may struggle with heavy rain or moving branches. Councils therefore need to assess reliability as well as projected electricity savings. Collecting movement data can also raise privacy questions. A system need not store identifiable journeys merely to activate a lamp, so planners should consider what data are genuinely necessary and how long they are retained. Technical capability is not, by itself, a reason to collect everything.

G. The emerging principle is not universal darkness, nor unlimited brightness. It is light that is sufficient for an identified purpose, used at the times and places where that purpose exists. Decisions involve trade-offs among accessibility, energy, ecology and public confidence. A single measurement such as lamp wattage cannot settle them. Trials are especially valuable when they include a clear baseline, alternatives and a plan for listening to people who use the area at different hours. Successful projects may look modest: a shield on one lamp, a warmer source beside a river, or a timetable that reflects real use. Their value lies in solving a particular problem rather than producing the brightest photograph.

groups.title: Passage 3 · Learning from work · Questions 29–40
groups.text:
A. When an organisation makes a mistake, managers often announce that they will create a culture of learning. The phrase sounds attractive, but it leaves a difficult question unanswered: what exactly should be learned, and from which events? An accident that occurred under unusual conditions may teach little about ordinary work. Conversely, a process that succeeds every day may contain vulnerabilities that remain invisible until several small changes occur together. Learning requires more than collecting stories about failure. It requires an explanation that links actions, circumstances and outcomes without pretending that participants possessed information which became available only afterwards.

B. Historian Lena Ortiz distinguishes between a useful account and a satisfying account. A satisfying account often identifies one careless individual and gives the organisation a simple remedy: replace that person or require more attention. A useful account asks why a decision made sense to the person at the time. This does not remove responsibility or imply that all behaviour is acceptable. Deliberate disregard of a known safety rule can still deserve a sanction. But if several competent employees independently make the same error, treating each one as an isolated exception may conceal a confusing instruction, an unrealistic deadline or an unreliable display. The point is to improve explanation before choosing an intervention.

C. A fictional hospital illustrates the distinction. Nurses twice selected the wrong package from a cupboard containing visually similar medicines. Both events were caught before a patient received the medicine. The initial proposal was a reminder to read labels more carefully. A review instead found that the two products occupied neighbouring shelves and that evening staff read small print under weak lighting. The hospital separated the products, enlarged shelf labels and improved the lamp. In six months of observation, no further selection error was reported. The review team nevertheless avoided claiming that the changes had eliminated the risk: reports could be incomplete and six months was a limited period. It continued to monitor near misses as well as actual harm.

D. Near misses can provide unusually rich information because the organisation can investigate them without the injury or damage of a completed accident. Yet employees may not report them if reporting leads automatically to blame. An anonymous reporting channel can help, although it makes follow-up questions harder. Another solution is to distinguish a confidential conversation about ordinary mistakes from the procedure for reckless behaviour. Trust develops through experience: employees watch what happens to colleagues who report problems. A poster promising openness has little effect if the first reporter loses a promotion. Managers must also respond visibly, since reports that disappear into a database can persuade staff that speaking up is pointless.

E. Collecting reports is therefore only the beginning. A review meeting can generate a long list of recommendations, but organisations often prefer those that are easy to announce rather than those that change work. Training is a common example. It is appropriate when knowledge is missing, yet additional training cannot repair a badly designed interface or provide staff with time that their schedules do not allow. Engineer Arun Vale proposes testing each recommendation against a question: would this change make the undesired action less likely even on a busy day? He also advises assigning an owner and a review date. Without these, a recommendation may remain officially accepted but practically absent.

F. Success deserves investigation too. A team may deliver a project on schedule only because experienced staff quietly compensate for gaps in the plan. If management interprets the result as proof that the plan needs no improvement, those compensations become normal expectations. The organisation loses the opportunity to learn about fragile conditions before somebody is unable to bridge them. Observing ordinary work helps reveal how tasks are actually completed rather than how a procedure says they should be completed. Such observation must be conducted respectfully. If employees believe the observer is searching for reasons to punish them, they may demonstrate an ideal procedure which conceals everyday adjustments.

G. There is no universal number of reports that demonstrates a healthy learning culture. A rising total might indicate more problems, greater willingness to disclose them, or both. A falling total might signal safer processes or growing silence. Interpretation requires several sources of evidence, including conversations, observations and the completion of improvement actions. Leaders should resist ranking departments by report counts alone. The most defensible goal is an organisation that notices weak signals, investigates them fairly and tests whether its response actually changes the conditions of work. In that sense, learning is an ongoing practice rather than a badge awarded after a training session.

groups.title: Part 3 · Matching headings · Questions 15–20
groups.text:
A. When a building is no longer required for its original purpose, demolition is not the only possible response. An old school can become a community centre, while a warehouse can house small businesses. This process is often called adaptive reuse. It can retain a familiar landmark and make use of materials already present. However, the age of a building does not automatically make reuse sensible. Planners must examine its condition, the intended use and the work needed to connect the two. An attractive exterior may hide a structure that needs extensive repair.

B. One advantage is that much of the energy once used to produce the building's materials need not be spent again on complete replacement. Reusing walls and floors can avoid the production and transport of new materials. These benefits vary greatly with the repairs required. A project that retains only the facade while replacing everything behind it is different from one that keeps most of the structure. Meaningful comparisons should include future energy use as well as construction. A poorly insulated building may need improvements before it is comfortable to occupy throughout the year.

C. Older buildings can be awkward to adapt. Corridors designed for schoolchildren may not suit equipment used by a business. A historic stairway may prevent wheelchair users from reaching upper floors. Engineers must consider fire safety, access and the load that floors can carry. Solving one problem sometimes creates another: installing a lift may remove space that the new users need. Early discussions among designers, future occupants and conservation specialists are therefore valuable. They help identify requirements while there is still time to change the plan rather than after expensive work has begun.

D. Financial decisions are rarely straightforward. A developer may compare the estimated cost of reuse with the cost of a new building but overlook uncertainty. Hidden damage can add expense after work starts. On the other hand, demolition can require waste disposal and delays for new permissions. The most useful budget therefore includes a contingency rather than pretending the first estimate is exact. Long-term demand also matters. A conversion designed for a single organisation may become empty if that organisation moves. Flexible rooms can make a building easier to let to different users later.

E. Residents do not always share the same view of a familiar building. Some value its history; others remember poor conditions and want a fresh start. Public discussion can reveal which features carry meaning, such as a hall used for celebrations or a courtyard where people gathered. Keeping these features may matter more to the community than preserving every internal partition. Consultation should include people who will use the building as well as those who live nearby. The aim is to understand competing needs, not simply count signatures supporting a predetermined design.

F. Successful reuse is therefore both a technical and a social achievement. It respects what is valuable without requiring the past to remain unchanged. There are cases where replacement is safer or more practical, and acknowledging them does not weaken the case for reuse elsewhere. Decisions improve when comparisons are transparent and outcomes are checked after occupation. Are the rooms being used? Can everybody access them? Are maintenance costs manageable? These questions turn a promising design into an accountable project and help the next team avoid repeating preventable mistakes.

groups.title: Part 4 · Detail and inference · Questions 21–29
groups.text:
A. Before the city of Bellhaven opened its first library of things, residents could borrow books but not the equipment needed to maintain their homes. Buying a drill for a single afternoon seemed wasteful, yet commercial hire shops mainly served professional builders and required expensive deposits. A neighbourhood survey found that householders were more interested in borrowing practical equipment than in attending additional workshops. The council therefore converted a vacant room beside the public library into a lending service. It opened in March 2017 with ninety donated objects, ranging from carpet cleaners to sewing machines. Its purpose was to reduce unnecessary purchases rather than to generate a profit. A small membership fee was introduced to pay for maintenance, but residents receiving certain benefits could join free.

B. The organisers initially predicted that gardening equipment would be most popular. In practice, carpet cleaners were requested more often than any other category. The result reflected the large number of rented flats in the area: tenants wanted to clean before moving out, while many had no garden. Some objects attracted surprisingly little interest. A pasta machine was borrowed twice in its first year, despite attracting many enthusiastic comments at the launch. Staff learned that what people admire publicly and what they actually need are not always the same. They began asking members about upcoming tasks rather than showing them attractive products and requesting opinions. This changed both purchasing decisions and the wording of publicity materials.

C. Borrowing rules also evolved. During the first six months, everything could be kept for seven days. Members complained that weekend-only projects did not require a whole week, whereas sewing projects sometimes took longer. The service eventually introduced different loan periods for different categories. A deposit remained compulsory for especially valuable items, but ordinary members did not need a deposit for basic tools. Late returns caused more difficulties than broken items: an object that appeared available online could still be in somebody's kitchen when the next borrower arrived. Automated reminders helped, but staff also reserved a day between consecutive bookings for inspections. Consequently, an item was not always bookable immediately after its scheduled return.

D. Maintaining the collection required expertise that the original volunteers did not all possess. Two retired engineers began a weekly repair session, and a local college supplied supervised students. The partnership gave students experience with genuine faults rather than carefully prepared classroom demonstrations. Every electrical item was inspected after each loan, even when the borrower reported no problem. Items that failed inspection were removed from the catalogue until repaired. The service did not invite members to mend electrical faults themselves. However, it offered a short introductory session on safe operation before lending unfamiliar equipment. Attendance was compulsory for some machines but optional for ordinary hand tools. Records of repairs gradually revealed which brands were economical over their entire working life, not merely cheap to acquire.

E. The environmental benefits were harder to establish than the borrowing statistics. A lending transaction does not automatically replace a purchase: without the service, some members might simply have postponed their project or borrowed from a relative. Researcher Maya Chen interviewed 120 members and asked what they would otherwise have done. She estimated that approximately half of the loans replaced purchases, while warning that the sample was voluntary and might overrepresent environmentally motivated residents. Her study did not compare Bellhaven with another city. Nor did it measure the energy used in manufacturing every object. Chen recommended reporting several indicators, including utilisation, repairs and avoided purchases, rather than presenting one impressive but uncertain carbon-saving figure.

F. In 2022, a grant allowed the service to extend its opening hours to two evenings a week. Members working during ordinary library hours then used it more often. The grant did not fund a larger collection; staff argued that access mattered more than adding objects which would sit unused. Membership rose, but the council declined an offer from a retailer to install advertisements in the borrowing room. Managers wanted advice to remain independent of sales. They still bought replacement items from several suppliers and published their selection principles. The next planned improvement was a shared reservation system with two nearby neighbourhoods. It would increase access to specialist equipment without requiring each branch to own an identical collection.

groups.title: Part 5 · Completion and choice · Questions 30–35
groups.text:
A. For decades, city administrations have treated street lighting as a straightforward question of visibility: brighter streets were assumed to be better streets. Yet the introduction of efficient LED lamps has reopened a more complicated debate. A lamp that consumes fewer watts can still produce a great deal of unwanted light. If its lower running cost encourages a city to install more lamps or operate them for longer, total energy savings may be smaller than predicted. Researchers call this a rebound effect. It does not mean that efficient technology is useless. It means that the benefits of efficiency depend partly on decisions made after installation, including how much illumination users consider necessary.

B. Light can be directed more precisely than older systems allowed. A well-designed fitting illuminates a pavement without sending much light into bedroom windows or directly into the sky. This distinction matters because total brightness is a poor description of lighting quality. A powerful lamp shining into a pedestrian's eyes can reduce the ability to see an uneven surface beyond it. Engineers describe such discomfort as glare. Shielding the source and controlling its angle may improve visibility even when measured output is lower. Some city councils now assess whether a light serves a specific task instead of applying the same standard to every street, park and car park.

C. Ecological concerns have also changed the discussion. Artificial light at night can alter the behaviour of insects, birds and other animals. In a fictional field trial near Lanton, researchers compared riverbank sites under three types of lamp. Blue-rich white lamps attracted more flying insects than warmer lamps, although the difference varied with weather. Removing lights altogether had a larger effect than changing their colour. The team emphasised that the experiment examined attraction to lamps, not long-term changes in insect populations. A lower count at a particular lamp therefore did not prove that more insects survived across the whole landscape. Similar care is needed when drawing conclusions about birds from observations on a single illuminated building.

D. Public safety is often invoked as a reason to resist dimming. However, correlations between lighting and recorded crime can be difficult to interpret. Wealthier districts may have both newer lights and other investments such as better transport or staffed public spaces. When a council changes lighting, it may also increase police patrols. A subsequent decline in crime cannot automatically be attributed to the lamps. This uncertainty does not justify ignoring residents' concerns. Rather, it suggests that evaluations should include comparable areas and record other changes during the study. Perceived safety also matters because fear can stop people using a route even when recorded incidents are rare. A technically efficient scheme that nobody trusts may fail in practice.

E. In the fictional town of Norbridge, a pilot project dimmed selected residential streetlights after midnight rather than switching them off. The council excluded road junctions and pedestrian crossings. Before the trial, residents walked the routes with engineers and identified places where trees blocked the light. Pruning branches solved several problems without adding brighter lamps. The council then collected feedback through both an online questionnaire and paper forms at the library, since an online-only survey would have excluded some residents. Most respondents accepted the dimming, but people working night shifts asked for a well-lit connection between the bus stop and the main road. That section was subsequently removed from the pilot.

F. Smart controls provide another possibility. Sensors can increase output when a pedestrian approaches and reduce it afterwards. Nevertheless, buying sensors introduces costs of its own: equipment must be maintained, software supported and faults investigated. A control system that works well in a demonstration may struggle with heavy rain or moving branches. Councils therefore need to assess reliability as well as projected electricity savings. Collecting movement data can also raise privacy questions. A system need not store identifiable journeys merely to activate a lamp, so planners should consider what data are genuinely necessary and how long they are retained. Technical capability is not, by itself, a reason to collect everything.

G. The emerging principle is not universal darkness, nor unlimited brightness. It is light that is sufficient for an identified purpose, used at the times and places where that purpose exists. Decisions involve trade-offs among accessibility, energy, ecology and public confidence. A single measurement such as lamp wattage cannot settle them. Trials are especially valuable when they include a clear baseline, alternatives and a plan for listening to people who use the area at different hours. Successful projects may look modest: a shield on one lamp, a warmer source beside a river, or a timetable that reflects real use. Their value lies in solving a particular problem rather than producing the brightest photograph.

You will hear the organiser of a town festival addressing volunteers. Look at questions eleven to twenty.

Welcome to the briefing for the Riverlight Festival. This year the festival will take place in the old market square. We originally planned to use the riverside field, but recent rain has made the ground unsuitable for heavy equipment. The market square has a firm surface and better access for deliveries. The programme has not changed, although some activities will be closer together than we intended. Please remember that residents still need to reach their homes around the square. Keeping the entrances clear is more important than arranging a perfectly straight row of stalls.

We expect visitors from eleven in the morning. Volunteers need to report at eight forty-five, not nine thirty. Several of you may have the earlier draft of the timetable, so please update it now. You will receive a badge at the information desk. Wear it throughout your shift: visitors and the emergency team need to identify you quickly. We will also issue radios to team leaders. Ordinary volunteers should contact their leader rather than trying to call every other team. This keeps urgent messages from being lost in too much conversation.

If you find a lost child, stay with the child and call the information desk. Do not walk around the festival looking for the family, and do not make an announcement yourself. The staff at the desk follow a specific procedure and contact security when necessary. For a minor injury, take the visitor to the first-aid tent beside the fountain. If somebody cannot move safely, contact your team leader and keep the area clear. The public announcement system is for urgent information, not for asking a colleague to bring lunch.

Here are the tasks for our five volunteer teams. The Red team will check tickets at the entrance. Some visitors have paper tickets and others have an electronic code; both are acceptable. Please direct anyone whose code cannot be read to the information desk. The Blue team is responsible for helping performers find the stage and their waiting area. Several visiting musicians do not know the town, so show them the route rather than simply pointing across the crowd.

The Green team will collect litter and replace full recycling bags. You are not expected to lift equipment or move tables. Tell a team leader if a bag contains something sharp. The Yellow team will provide information at the desk. Please study the programme and know where the accessible toilets are. The Purple team will look after the children's craft area. Parents must remain with their children; volunteers are helping with the activity, not providing a childcare service. If a parent tries to leave, explain this rule politely.

Some volunteers have asked about money. Food sellers deal with their own payments. None of our five teams will handle stall income. Equally, transport to and from the station is being managed by the council, so no festival volunteer is assigned to the station bus. These two tasks were included on an early list, which is why I want to make the distinction clear today.

You will have a twenty-minute break during each shift. Agree the time with your leader so that the entire team does not leave together. Water is available behind the information desk. The festival finishes at five, but visitors may take time to leave. Please wait until your leader says your work is complete. We do not want bags or barriers removed while visitors still need the routes. Finally, there will be a short review next week. Tell us what worked and what could be improved; good reports help us plan next year's event.

groups.title: Part 3 · Student research · Questions 21–30
groups.script:
You will hear two students discussing a research project with their tutor. Look at questions twenty-one to thirty.

We've brought our project plan about food waste on campus. Our first idea was to compare the university with local restaurants, but that would require permission from too many businesses. We've narrowed the project to waste in the campus dining halls. A sensible choice. What do you want to find out? Whether smaller plates reduce the amount students leave after lunch. We don't want to suggest that students eat less; we're interested in whether the serving arrangement affects leftovers. Good. Define your outcome clearly before you start collecting data.

We thought about asking students to estimate their own waste in a survey. That could tell you about attitudes, but not reliably about quantities. People may not remember accurately, and those who feel embarrassed could understate the amount. We will weigh the leftovers instead. We can separate food from packaging at the collection point. Yes, make sure you distinguish edible leftovers from bones and peels. Otherwise a change in the menu could look like a change in behaviour. We've arranged a short training session for the people who collect the trays so they all follow the same procedure.

How will you compare plate sizes? For the first week, dining hall North will use the ordinary plates while South uses smaller ones. Then we switch them for the second week. Keeping each hall permanently in one condition would be simpler, but the halls attract different students. Exactly. Switching helps you avoid confusing a hall's usual customers with the effect of its plates. It doesn't remove every problem, so describe the limitations. We plan to keep the main menu identical in the two halls. Students can still choose among the options, but the available dishes should be the same.

What about attendance? We'll count the diners. Comparing total waste would be misleading if one hall serves twice as many lunches. We should calculate waste per diner. That's important. Also note special events. If a sports group arrives in only one hall on one day, its eating habits might influence the result. We can record the event in our notes rather than quietly removing that day's data. Good. Your report should explain any exclusion of data, and the rule should be decided before you see whether the result helps your hypothesis.

We asked the dining staff about practical difficulties. They said students sometimes carry food out, so not all leftovers return on a tray. We'll explain that we measure waste returned to the hall, not every piece of food students discard anywhere. Will you photograph the trays? No. We don't need images of people or their meals to weigh leftovers. We will use anonymous counts and ask the ethics office to review the procedure. That is more appropriate than collecting names and deleting them later.

For our information sources, we found a newspaper article which claims that smaller plates always work. Don't use that as your main evidence. It can introduce the topic, but you should examine the research behind the claim. We found a journal review that compares studies and explains why results differ. That is a better starting point for the literature section. We'll also interview the catering manager about how feasible a permanent change would be. The interview won't establish whether the plates reduce waste, but it can explain practical constraints.

We have three weeks until the presentation. We should collect data next week, analyse it during the following week and prepare the slides in the final week. Send me your final data sheet by Friday before you begin. Check the units and categories now: changing them halfway through would make comparison difficult. You should also test the scales with a known weight each day. Thank you. We'll run a small pilot tomorrow to check the collection procedure before the main study.

groups.title: Part 4 · Peatland lecture · Questions 31–40
groups.script:
You will hear a lecture about restoring peatlands. Look at questions thirty-one to forty.

Today's lecture concerns peatlands, landscapes in which partially decomposed plant material accumulates over long periods. The key condition is waterlogging. When ground remains saturated, there is little oxygen available below the surface, and decomposition slows. Plant material can consequently accumulate as peat instead of being broken down rapidly. This process does not happen at the same rate everywhere, so an apparently similar surface can conceal very different depths and histories. A peatland is therefore not simply a wet field; it is a system in which water, vegetation and accumulated material interact.

Peatlands can store a large amount of carbon. Draining them for farming or other uses lowers the water table and allows oxygen to enter layers that were previously saturated. Decomposition then increases and stored carbon can be released into the atmosphere. Dry peat can also burn. Fires may continue below the visible surface, which makes them difficult to detect and extinguish. Restoring a peatland often begins by raising the water table rather than by planting a decorative collection of flowers. Without suitable water conditions, the intended vegetation may fail to establish and the underlying loss of peat may continue.

A common restoration action is to block old drainage ditches with dams. The dams may be made from peat or other suitable material, depending on the site. Their purpose is to slow the escape of water, not to create a deep lake over the entire landscape. Hydrology must be studied carefully because a poorly placed barrier can flood neighbouring land or direct water along a new channel. Teams also need to understand who owns and uses the land. Agreements with farmers and nearby residents are part of restoration, not an optional addition after engineering work has been finished.

Another action is to protect bare peat from erosion. In a fictional trial on Glen Moss, workers covered selected damaged surfaces with heather cuttings. The cuttings reduced exposure to wind and helped trap moisture. Elsewhere, they replanted small patches of moss taken from a healthy part of the same site under a conservation permit. The project was not a claim that one planting method would work everywhere. It was a comparison of methods in a particular place. Areas receiving no treatment were included so the team could distinguish a treatment effect from a wet season which improved all plots.

How should success be measured? The most immediate indicator is often the water level. Teams place instruments in the ground and measure the depth of the water table repeatedly. A single reading after heavy rain can be misleading. Measurements across seasons are more informative, and they can reveal whether a dam is leaking during dry weather. Vegetation surveys provide a second indicator, but a green surface alone does not prove that peat accumulation has resumed. Some fast-growing grasses tolerate conditions quite different from those required by peat-forming mosses.

Gas measurements add another complication. Rewetting may reduce carbon dioxide emissions from decomposition while temporarily increasing methane emissions. It is therefore important to consider the whole balance over time rather than celebrating a reduction in one gas and ignoring another. Researchers use models and repeated observations to estimate the climate effect. Their conclusions depend on assumptions about future conditions, so reports should make those assumptions explicit. Restoration benefits can also include cleaner water, reduced erosion and habitat improvement, even when the climate calculation remains uncertain.

Finally, these landscapes develop slowly. A dam can be installed in a day, but a functioning peat-forming ecosystem may take many years to recover. Funding that covers only construction and one follow-up visit is unlikely to demonstrate lasting success. Projects need a monitoring plan, responsibility for repairs and a way to learn from sites where recovery is slower than expected. Restoration is not achieved when the last machine leaves. It is achieved through sustained changes in water conditions and ecological processes, supported by long-term care.

Welcome to the newly renovated community garden. I will describe the layout so you can find the facilities. Look at the plan while you listen. You enter at the south, where the entrance is shown at the bottom. The main path runs north from the entrance to a round fountain in the centre. A second path crosses from west to east through that fountain. The letters on the plan mark the locations; they are not the names of the facilities.

The structure at the east end of that cross path is used for maintenance equipment, not refreshments.

If you follow the main path north past the fountain, there are two larger areas at the far end. The playground is in the northwest corner. It has a low fence and is separate from the vegetable plots, so children can play without damaging plants. Parents should stay with their children, as our volunteers cannot supervise them. The northeast corner is occupied by the greenhouse. The greenhouse is open during guided tours, but otherwise please look from the path. Its doors must remain closed to keep the temperature stable.

There are also two small buildings in the middle of the upper half of the garden. The accessible toilets are on the west side of the path, between the cafe and the playground. On the east side, between the maintenance area and the greenhouse, there is a teaching room. Classes meet there when the weather is poor. The room is not a public shelter during an ordinary visit, because equipment is sometimes left out for a lesson. Notice that both buildings are closer to the fountain than the two corner areas. If you are unsure, ask at the information hut rather than entering a locked building.

Before you explore, please remember to stay on the paths unless a volunteer invites you onto a growing plot. Some newly planted areas look empty but contain seeds. Bicycles must be left outside the entrance. Dogs are welcome on leads, except inside the greenhouse and the children's area. groups.title: Part 6 · Urban trees · Questions 30–35
groups.script:
Today I will introduce a school project studying urban trees. The project is designed to help students collect useful observations rather than simply memorise tree names. Each team studies one street. Teams record the location of each tree and estimate the width of its trunk. The essential measuring tool is a tape. We use flexible measuring tapes, not rulers, because a tape can be wrapped around the trunk. Students should record the circumference at a height of one metre above the ground, unless an unusual shape makes that impossible. In that case they should write a note describing the problem.

Students also observe the leaves. Leaf shape can help identify a species, but colour alone is unreliable because it changes with season and health. For the first survey, we ask students to work in pairs. One person measures while the other writes, and then they exchange roles. Working alone is possible later, once the method is familiar. The aim is not to complete the longest list in the class but to collect measurements another team could check. Accuracy matters more than speed.

Teams should avoid measuring trees on private property without permission. Our first route includes only trees beside public pavements. There is no need to enter gardens or climb over fences. We have agreed the route with the school and the local authority. A teacher will accompany each group because some trees are beside busy roads. Students must keep away from the edge of the road while concentrating on their observations.

The observations are entered into a shared spreadsheet. Before entering data, every team checks that all measurements use the same unit. We record circumference in centimetres. Mixing metres and centimetres would create false differences between trees. The spreadsheet also has a notes column for damaged bark, missing branches and any uncertainty about species. An uncertain identification should be marked as uncertain rather than replaced by a confident guess. We can ask a local specialist to review these cases afterwards.

The second survey takes place in September. By returning to the same trees, students can compare observations over time. Growth over a few months may be too small for our method to detect, but changes in leaves or damage can still be interesting. We do not claim that the class survey measures the carbon stored in each tree precisely. That would require additional information and a validated model. Our project is about careful observation, consistent records and asking questions that the available evidence can answer. At the end, teams will prepare a short poster for the school exhibition showing their method, findings and limitations.
